title: Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Bill 2017
short_title: Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Bill 2017

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would redefine marriage as a union of two people, removing the current restriction to a man and a woman.
It would recognise same-sex marriages performed overseas and create a new category of religious marriage celebrants who can refuse to solemnise marriages against their beliefs.
Religious bodies would be allowed to refuse facilities, goods or services consistently with their doctrine, matching existing exemptions under the Sex Discrimination Act 1984.
changes: Redefines marriage to a union of two people regardless of sex or gender.
Allows ministers of religion to refuse to solemnise marriages that conflict with their religious doctrine.
Extends the exemption in the Sex Discrimination Act to cover conduct authorised by the Marriage Act.
summary.affected: Ministers of religion, religious marriage celebrants, bodies established for religious purposes, and same-sex couples.

The majority voted in favour of keeping particular parts of [schedule 1](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22legislation%2Fbills%2Fs1099_first-senate%2F0001%22;rec=0) unchanged. In parliamentary jargon, they voted for "*section 39DD and subsection 39DE(3) in item 8, and items 9 to 16 and 57, of schedule 1 [to] stand as printed.*" This division took place after Liberal Senator [David Fawcett](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/sa/david_fawcett) moved that that parts [be opposed](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2017-11-28.16.1). These parts deal with the issue of religious marriage celebrants (including how to identify them), who are allowed to discriminate on the basis of their religious beliefs in certain circumstances. ### Why did some Liberals vote Yes and others No? The Liberal Party was split on this issue, with some voting Yes and others voting No. This split within the party is unusual but, given the nature of the subject matter of the vote, the Liberal Party decided to run this as a free vote, meaning that its members could vote however they chose rather than having to vote along party lines. ### What does this bill do? This [bill](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/s1099) will allow same-sex couples to marry under Australian law. However, it will also: > *enable ministers of religion, religious marriage celebrants, chaplains and bodies established for religious purposes to refuse to solemnise or provide facilities, goods and services for marriages on religious grounds; and make amendments ... to provide that a refusal by a minister of religion, religious marriage celebrant or chaplain to solemnise marriage in prescribed circumstances does not constitute unlawful discrimination.* Read more in the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1718a/18bd054).

The majority voted against [amendments](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2017-11-28.147.1) introduced by Liberal Senators [David Fawcett](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/sa/david_fawcett) and [James Paterson](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/victoria/james_paterson). ### What do these amendments do? Senator Paterson [explained three of the most significant amendments](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2017-11-28.147.1), which he described as being about freedom of speech, antidetriment and parental rights. ### Why did some Liberals vote Yes and others No? Hastie MP explained that his amendments are important: > *because they seek to safeguard sincere Australians and entities that, for either conscientious or religion reasons, hold to a relevant marriage belief and directly associated beliefs on family structure, sexual relations and parenting. The amendments impose limitations on the expression of those marriage beliefs in that they must not constitute hate speech. They must not be harassing or threatening on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity, intersex status or marital or relationship status. They do not give licence to sexual discrimination. They do not permit a person or entity to discriminate against other Australians, as prohibited under the [Sex Discrimination Act 1984](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_Discrimination_Act_1984).* > *These amendments, rather, are a shield for people and organisations that hold to a traditional view of marriage. speeches.speaker: Trevor Evans
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that Parliament should pass the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Bill 2017 in a businesslike manner, noting that 79.5% of Brisbane voters supported same-sex marriage in the postal survey and that the bill strikes a balance between marriage equality and religious protections.

speeches.speaker: Tim Wilson
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Bill 2017, arguing it would end the marginalisation of same-sex couples and expand the freedom to marry while protecting religious freedom and free speech, and noted the 76.3% "yes" vote from his electorate of Goldstein.

speeches.speaker: Mark Dreyfus
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Bill 2017, passed by the Senate with 43 votes in favour and 12 against, should be passed unamended by the House of Representatives to deliver marriage equality as supported by a majority of Australians. Specific protections for religious celebrants and bodies were read out, and the speaker thanked senators including Penny Wong, Louise Pratt, Dean Smith, and Janet Rice, as well as advocates like Anna Brown, Rodney Croome, and Alex Greenwich.

speeches.speaker: Terri Butler
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Bill 2017 is an acceptable compromise that will finally allow same-sex marriage, while acknowledging the hurt caused by years of delay and the postal survey, which resulted in a 40% spike in mental health service demand for LGBTI people. They credited Labor figures including Bill Shorten, Louise Pratt, Penny Wong, and others for advancing marriage equality, and noted the bill creates new religious exemptions for civil celebrants.

speeches.speaker: Chris Hayes
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Marriage Amendment Bill, arguing that the national survey result obliges parliament to enact marriage equality, while religious freedom concerns should be addressed separately by the expert panel led by Philip Ruddock.

speeches.speaker: Warren Snowdon
speeches.brief: The speaker announced they will vote for the Marriage Amendment Bill 2017, arguing it is a cross-party parliamentary initiative, not a government one, and criticised the Prime Minister's characterisation of the debate as ungracious. They opposed amendments to protect religious freedom, citing a letter from Anglican bishops, and highlighted the postal survey's flaws, noting a 50.1% participation rate in their electorate of Lingiari and low engagement among Aboriginal communities and young people.

speeches.speaker: Anthony Albanese
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Bill 2017, arguing it would not affect religious freedom but would strengthen marriage by allowing same-sex couples to marry, and noted that the Australian people led the parliament through the postal ballot.

speeches.speaker: Christopher Pyne
speeches.brief: The speaker moved to suspend standing orders to allow the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Bill 2017 to be debated in government time, extend the sitting until midnight, defer divisions until 9:30 am on 6 December 2017, and delay any quorum count until the following morning.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Wallace
speeches.brief: The member for Fisher announced his support for the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Bill 2017, citing the 61.6% national and 62.8% local support in the postal survey, and argued for stronger protections of religious freedoms for the nearly five million Australians who voted no. He also criticised Labor and the Greens for blocking the plebiscite.

speeches.speaker: Cathy O'Toole
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Bill 2017 without amendments, noting that 62.8% of the Herbert electorate (48,110 people) voted yes in the postal survey, and criticised the $122 million spent on the survey.

speeches.speaker: Linda Burney
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Bill 2017, favouring marriage equality and opposing amendments that would roll back anti-discrimination protections. The speaker criticised the postal survey as expensive, divisive and hurtful, and noted that while the electorate of Barton returned a 'no' vote, the speaker had consistently supported equality.

speeches.speaker: Sussan Ley
speeches.brief: The electorate of Farrer voted 55% in favour of same-sex marriage in the postal survey, with a 77.4% participation rate. The speaker supported the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Bill 2017, citing local advocates including Georgia Henderson, Toni Johnson of Hume Phoenix, Archdeacon Peter Macleod Miller, and Hay Mardi Gras organiser Kerry Aldred, and noted that a review of religious freedom protections led by Philip Ruddock will report in March 2018.

speeches.speaker: Richard Marles
speeches.brief: The speaker argued in favour of the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Bill 2017, noting that 84% of Corio electors participated in the postal survey and 68% voted yes, and named Magda Szubanski as a key campaign figure. They also called for protecting religious freedoms and quoted Thomas Marshall on the meaning of marriage equality.

speeches.speaker: John McVeigh
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the traditional definition of marriage, citing his own 30-year Catholic marriage, while respecting differing views and noting that the same-sex marriage survey returned an emphatic 'yes' in Queensland. He also highlighted that local priorities in his electorate of Groom include the economy, jobs, and infrastructure like the Toowoomba Second Range Crossing.

speeches.speaker: Ian Goodenough
speeches.brief: The speaker tabled the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Human Rights’ scrutiny reports 12 and 13 of 2017 and annual reports for 2014–15 and 2015–16, noting that since the 45th Parliament commenced in August 2016 the committee examined 405 bills and 2,942 instruments, with 309 bills and 2,875 instruments assessed as promoting or permissibly limiting human rights or not engaging human rights.

speeches.speaker: Ian Goodenough
speeches.brief: The speaker announced he would vote for same-sex marriage based on the 68% yes vote in his electorate of Moore, despite his personal belief that marriage is for biological parents raising children. He argued the bill needs amendments to protect freedom of speech, religion, parental rights, and faith-based organisations, citing 4,873,987 no voters and examples like legal action against Archbishop Porteous.

speeches.speaker: Tim Hammond
speeches.brief: The speaker announced they would vote yes on the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Bill 2017, urging no amendments, no excuses and no more delays, and noted a 63.7% yes vote in Western Australia and 71.5% in their electorate of Perth.

speeches.speaker: Lisa Chesters
speeches.brief: The speaker announced they would vote yes on marriage equality and oppose the Prime Minister and member for Warringah's amendments, arguing those amendments would allow businesses like florists and taxis to discriminate against same-sex couples, which they said is wrong and comparable to outlawed racial discrimination.

speeches.speaker: Christopher Pyne
speeches.brief: The speaker argued in support of the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Bill 2017, stating that marriage equality is consistent with liberal and conservative values, and that denying same-sex couples the right to marry perpetuates discrimination. The speaker noted 45,000 Australian households with children of same-sex couples would benefit, and affirmed that religious protections in the bill are adequate, opposing unnecessary amendments.

speeches.speaker: Peter Khalil
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Bill 2017 should pass, citing the clear 'yes' vote in the postal survey (61.6% nationally, 70% in his electorate of Wills), and opposed any amendments that would weaken existing anti-discrimination laws, while noting the $122 million postal survey was a wasteful abrogation of parliamentary responsibility.

speeches.speaker: Ken O'Dowd
speeches.brief: The member for Flynn announced he would vote for the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Bill 2017, citing the 2016 election promise and the 62% national yes vote in the postal survey, with 76% of his electorate supporting the change.

speeches.speaker: Clare O'Neil
speeches.brief: The speaker argued in support of the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Bill 2017, calling it a significant step toward equality for LGBTIQ Australians. They praised groups like Rainbow Labor and young people, particularly 18- to 19-year-old women with 82% turnout, for their role in the campaign, while criticising the plebiscite process as harmful and noting that some opponents held a fundamental belief that being gay is wrong.

speeches.speaker: Paul Fletcher
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Bill 2017, citing the postal survey’s 80% participation and 61.6% national yes vote (60.6% in Bradfield), and criticised Labor for opposing the survey and delaying reform. He also stressed respecting the over five million no voters, including through a separate religious freedom inquiry led by Philip Ruddock.

speeches.speaker: George Christensen
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the same-sex marriage bill must include protections for religious freedom, freedom of speech, conscience, and parental rights, citing examples from Denmark, Sweden, the UK, New Zealand, and Australia where religious believers faced penalties or discrimination. He supported the bill only if these protections were added, noting that 55% of his electorate voted yes but nine out of 20 had concerns about freedoms.

acts.title: Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Act 2017
